prompt.context: Our client is a defense aircraft manufacturer based in the United States. They are negotiating the price of radiator fins, which are used to cool aircraft engines, with an existing supplier who has been supplying these parts for the last 10 years.
prompt.question: What should be an appropriate price for a radiator fin? Help the client prepare for this negotiation.

clarifying_info.a: They are a defense aircraft manufacturer.

clarifying_info.q: Who is the client negotiating with?
clarifying_info.a: They are negotiating with an existing supplier who has been supplying these products for the last 10 years.
They are based in the United States.

clarifying_info.q: What is the function of a radiator fin in a defense aircraft?
clarifying_info.a: Radiator fins are used for cooling the aircraft engines.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific leverage that our client has in this negotiation?
clarifying_info.a: By regulation, defense manufacturers can obtain the cost structure from their suppliers.

clarifying_info.q: How many suppliers are there in the market?
clarifying_info.a: Our client's supplier is the only one in the market.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a substitute product for radiator fins?
clarifying_info.a: No, the client cannot substitute radiator fins with any other product.

clarifying_info.q: What is the value proposition of this product?
clarifying_info.a: The radiator fins are essential for the aircraft to function.

framework: Industry Analysis: Assess market structure, number of suppliers, substitutes, and competitive dynamics

Pricing Strategy — three lenses: (1) Market-based pricing driven by competition; (2) Value-based pricing driven by the product's worth to the buyer; (3) Cost-based pricing driven by the supplier's cost structure and margin
Because there is only one supplier and no substitutes, market-based pricing is not applicable
Because the client is a defense manufacturer with regulatory access to supplier cost data, cost-based pricing is the primary lever

Cost structure of the supplier should be broken into components: Raw Material (driver: market price), Labor (driver: geography/labor market), SG&A including overhead (driver: efficiency), Allocated fixed cost (driver: utilization/scale), Transportation (driver: distance, weight, volume, mode)

questions.prompt: Walk through the cost-based pricing calculation using the data provided. The supplier's current (old) cost structure is: Material $300, Labor $100, SG&A 13% of production costs. Transportation is $5,000 per box of 12 fins, and the supplier's margin is 20%. What is the current price per fin?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build up cost per fin step by step: production costs first, then transportation per fin, then apply margin on top of the full cost. Strong candidates will also challenge whether the old cost structure itself is accurate before calculating the new price.

math.setup: Old cost structure: Material=$300, Labor=$100, SG&A=13% of (Material+Labor), Transportation=$5,000/box with 12 fins/box, Margin=20% applied multiplicatively on top of total cost.

questions.prompt: The supplier has proposed new cost inputs: Material costs have increased by 7%, Labor costs have decreased by 2%, Transportation costs have decreased by 12%. SG&A remains at 13% of production costs and margin remains at 20%. What is the new fair price per fin?
questions.guidance: Candidate applies percentage changes to each line item and recalculates bottom-up. A strong candidate notes that margin should not be applied on top of transportation if transportation is a pass-through cost, and flags this as a risk/assumption.

math.setup: Apply changes: Material = $300 × 1.07, Labor = $100 × 0.98, SG&A = 13% of new (Material+Labor), Transportation = ($5,000/12) × 0.88, Margin = 20% on total cost.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the components and drivers of a supplier's cost structure for a manufactured part like a radiator fin?

categories.name: Raw Material
ideas: Driven by prevalent market price of metals/alloys
Hedging or long-term supply contracts can stabilize cost

categories.name: Labor
ideas: Driven by geography and local labor market conditions

categories.name: SG&A / Overhead
ideas: Facility costs allocated to this product line

categories.name: Allocated Fixed Costs
ideas: Driven by capacity utilization and production scale
Higher utilization lowers per-unit fixed cost

categories.name: Transportation
ideas: Driven by geographical distance between supplier and client

recommendation: Based on cost-based pricing analysis, the fair price for a radiator fin under the new cost structure is approximately $1,008 per fin, down from the current $1,042
The client should negotiate the price down to $1,008 and use the regulatory right to access the supplier's cost breakdown as leverage
risks: The 20% margin was applied on top of transportation cost — if transportation is treated as a pass-through rather than a margin-bearing cost, the final price would be different
The old cost structure has not been independently verified; the actual baseline may differ, which would change the negotiated target
Single-supplier dependency means the client has limited walk-away power despite cost transparency rights
next_steps: Conduct cost modeling to validate the accuracy of the old (baseline) cost structure before entering negotiations
Request full cost breakdown documentation from the supplier as permitted by defense regulations
Explore whether any long-term supply agreement terms (volume, duration) could be renegotiated alongside price
